status_reasoning: Reviewers affirm that "the work is of very high quality" and "the conclusions drawn about the shape of the complex, the location of the different subunits and the relative orientation of the subunits are sound and convincing." They note the structure is "a very significant advance" and that conclusions are "supported by redundant and accurate information." The cross-linking experiments are said to "confirm the structural conclusions."

Reviewers note that "the original images show a heterogeneous population of particles and in particular smaller particles that suggest that some particles may dissociate." They request clarification on "whether all particles were considered or whether some were rejected" and ask for rejection criteria to be communicated, indicating concern about sample heterogeneity and particle selection.

Reviewers question the methodological choice, asking "why only 20 classes were considered for the Random Conical Tilt method," noting this "would correspond to an angular difference of 40 or 50 degrees between classes which is a large merging angle and would lead to a rather poor resolution." They request justification for this decision.

Reviewers state that "the authors make a number of suggestions to provide a structural basis for previous biochemical observations" including "the stabilization of the complex by AEBP1" but note "these inferences about biochemical function are speculative given the resolution of the structure." The allosteric role and stabilization mechanism are considered interpretive rather than definitively established.

Reviewers explicitly state that "the authors make a number of suggestions to provide a structural basis for previous biochemical observations. These include how the enzymatic activity is affected by modifications of the H3 tail" but emphasize "these inferences about biochemical function are speculative given the resolution of the structure." The mechanistic interpretations about regulation are considered speculative rather than conclusively demonstrated.

Reviewers directly challenge these claims, stating "the conclusions of the manuscript, and in particular the functional consequences for the interaction of PRC2 with nucleosomes, are highly speculative. The histone tails that interact with the WD40 repeats of PRC2 are extremely flexible and one cannot conclude at this stage that PRC2 will bind between two adjacent nucleosomes." They request removal of related discussion about linker histone H1 interactions.

Reviewers affirm that "the cross-linking experiments confirm the structural conclusions" and note the work reaches "important conclusions supported by redundant and accurate information." The cross-linking and mass spectrometry data identifying protein-protein contacts and domain localizations are accepted as sound and convincing evidence for subunit organization.

These background and contextual claims about PRC2 function, importance, and prior knowledge are not questioned by reviewers. Reviewers acknowledge that "PRC2 is of fundamental importance and high interest" and that this work represents "a very significant advance over previous high-resolution structures of isolated domains," implicitly accepting the background context.
